The sector model of urban development, proposed by economist Homer Hoyt in 1939,
illustrates how a city's residential areas grow in relation to its center and major
transportation routes, such as highways. According to this model, cities expand outward in
distinct sectors or wedges from the central business district (CBD), with each sector
representing different types of residential environments, such as low-income or middle-
class neighborhoods. Major highways influence this growth by providing easy access to
various sectors, encouraging people to move outward from the city center into areas that
align with their socioeconomic status. As a result, the sector model helps explain the
spatial organization of urban areas, highlighting the relationship between transportation
and residential patterns.
answers.explanation: The answer correctly identifies the sector model's key premise that cities develop in wedge-shaped sectors based on proximity to the central business district and major transportation routes, which dictate the distribution of different residential areas.
